questions.q: A marketing manager asks Claude to 'write something about our product.' The output is generic. What is the MOST effective first improvement?
opts: Ask Claude to try again
Add specific context: audience, tone, format, and key product details
Switch to a larger model
Shorten the prompt so Claude focuses better
questions.exp: A generic request gets a generic answer, and no amount of retrying changes that: the model is filling in the gaps you left with the most average plausible content. What turns it around is supplying the information only you have - who is reading this, what they already believe, what the product actually does, what a good result looks like. That is why bigger models rarely fix this class of problem: capability was never the constraint, context was. Shortening the prompt makes it worse for the same reason. The useful instinct to build here is that vague output is usually a symptom of a vague brief, not a weak model.
why: Retrying resamples the same underspecified request. You may get different generic text, but nothing has been added for the model to work from.
Correct. Audience, tone, format and product specifics are the information the model cannot infer, and supplying them is what makes the output specific.
A larger model reasons better over what it is given. It cannot know your audience or your product details, so it produces more polished generic copy.
Brevity is not the problem. Cutting words removes context, which is the opposite of what an underspecified prompt needs.

questions.q: Which prompting technique is BEST when you need Claude to follow a precise output structure every time?
opts: Asking politely and repeating the request
Providing an explicit template or example of the desired output
Using all caps for important words
Keeping the prompt under one sentence
questions.exp: Structure is easier to demonstrate than to describe. A filled-in example fixes the section order, the heading style, the level of detail, and the treatment of edge cases all at once - and it does so unambiguously, where prose descriptions leave room for interpretation that shows up as drift across runs. This is also why examples are the strongest signal in a prompt and should be chosen carefully: the model matches their length and tone as readily as their shape, so an example that is longer or more formal than you want will pull the output that way. One good example usually beats three paragraphs explaining the same format.
why: Politeness and repetition do not encode structure. Repeating an ambiguous instruction just states the ambiguity twice.
Correct. A worked example pins down order, depth and formatting at once, with none of the interpretive room that a description leaves.
Capitals signal emphasis, not structure, and heavy emphasis tends to distort the response rather than shape it.
A one-sentence prompt has less room to specify structure, not more. Constraints have to be stated somewhere.

questions.q: You want Claude to reason carefully through a complex analysis before answering. What actually controls that?
opts: Telling it to think step by step in the prompt
The thinking setting on the request, and how much effort you allow it
Writing the prompt in a formal tone
Asking the same question several times and comparing
questions.exp: Reasoning depth is a property of the request, not a phrase in the prompt. Current models use adaptive thinking, meaning Claude decides how much to think per request, and you steer the depth with an effort setting. Asking a model to think step by step was a real technique on models that did not reason by default; on current ones it changes the wording of the answer, not whether the model reasons. What the prompt genuinely controls is the quality of the input: the task, the constraints, and what a good answer looks like.
why: A prompt phrase does not switch reasoning on. This was sound advice for older models and is now the most common piece of dated prompting guidance still in circulation.
Correct. Thinking is configured on the request, with effort setting the depth, and Claude decides how much reasoning each specific request needs.
Tone affects register, not reasoning. A formal prompt does not buy a more careful answer.
Repeating a question gives you several samples at the same reasoning depth, for several times the cost. It is a check, not a control.

questions.q: When giving Claude a long document plus instructions, the most reliable structure is:
opts: Mix the instructions through the document so they stay near the relevant text
Document first inside clear delimiters, then the instruction at the end
Paste the document with no framing and ask afterwards
Summarise the document yourself first, always
questions.exp: Two things matter and they work together. Delimit the document, with XML-style tags as the convention, so the model can tell source material from instruction; without that boundary, text inside the document can read as a command, which is also how prompt injection gets in. Then put the actual ask at the end, closest to where generation begins, which measurably improves instruction-following on long inputs. Summarising the document yourself defeats the purpose: you have done the reading, and your summary is what gets analysed rather than the source.
why: Scattering instructions makes it ambiguous which text is a command and which is content, and leaves no single place to look when the output is wrong.
Correct. Delimiters separate source from task, and an instruction at the end sits closest to generation, which helps most on long inputs.
With no framing the model has to infer both the task and the boundary of the source, and it will sometimes infer wrong.
Occasionally useful, never a rule, and it shifts the analysis onto your summary rather than the document itself.

questions.q: Claude produces a confident summary citing a statistic you can't find in the source document. What should you do?
opts: Trust it — Claude is usually right
Verify against the source; treat unsupported claims as potential hallucinations
Ask Claude if it is sure, and accept its answer
Publish with a disclaimer
questions.exp: An unsupported figure is the highest-risk output a model produces, because fluent prose gives a fabricated number the same authority as a real one. The rule that holds up is source-first: a claim that cannot be traced to the document does not go out, whatever the surrounding text sounds like. Asking the model whether it is sure is worse than useless - self-assessment is generated the same way the original claim was, so a confident retraction and a confident confirmation cost exactly the same. A disclaimer does not help either: it transfers the risk to the reader rather than removing it, and readers do not verify.
why: Usually right is not a standard you can apply to an individual claim, and the ones that are wrong look identical to the ones that are right.
Correct. Trace it to the source, and treat anything unsupported as a potential fabrication until confirmed.
Self-assessment is generated by the same process that produced the claim. It adds confidence, not evidence.
A disclaimer moves responsibility to the reader without making the number any more true, and most readers will not check.

questions.q: Which is the BEST routine practice for evaluating Claude's output on high-stakes work?
opts: Spot-check every fifth response
Human review of facts, logic, and tone before use, especially for external audiences
Run the same prompt twice and use the longer answer
Rely on Claude's self-assessment
questions.exp: High-stakes work needs review that is systematic rather than statistical, because the failures are not evenly distributed - a fabricated citation or an inverted conclusion can sit inside otherwise excellent output. Reviewing facts, logic and tone before anything reaches an external audience is the control that actually catches those. Sampling every fifth response assumes errors arrive at a predictable rate, which is exactly what makes it unsafe for work where one bad output is the problem. Comparing two runs measures consistency, not correctness, and two confidently wrong answers agree with each other perfectly.
why: Sampling catches systemic drift but is designed to miss individual errors, which is the failure mode that matters when the output is high-stakes.
Correct. Facts, logic and tone reviewed by a human before use, with the bar rising for anything leaving the organisation.
Length is not a quality signal, and running twice measures consistency rather than correctness - two wrong answers can agree.
Asking the model to grade itself produces more generated text, not independent verification.

questions.q: Claude gives you a plausible-looking legal citation. The safest assumption is:
opts: Citations are always real
It may be fabricated and must be independently verified
Only page numbers can be wrong
It's real if it appears twice
questions.exp: Citations are the single most dangerous output category, because their format is highly regular and their content is not verifiable from the text itself. A plausible case name, court and year is exactly what a language model is good at producing whether or not the case exists - and legal citations have produced real professional sanctions for exactly this reason. Treat every citation as unverified until you have found the source itself. Repetition is not corroboration either: the same prompt asked twice draws on the same patterns, so a fabricated citation reproduces happily.
why: Citation format is easy to imitate and impossible to verify from the text, so real and fabricated citations look identical on the page.
Correct. Assume it may be fabricated and confirm it against the source before relying on it.
The case, court and year can all be wrong. Restricting doubt to page numbers understates the failure mode considerably.
Appearing twice reflects a consistent pattern in the output, not a verified fact. Repetition is not corroboration.

questions.q: A good technique to make Claude's outputs easier to verify is to ask it to:
opts: Be more confident
Quote or cite the specific source passages it relied on
Use more technical jargon
Avoid mentioning sources to save tokens
questions.exp: Asking for the supporting passage changes what you have to check. Instead of assessing whether a claim sounds right - which is exactly the judgement fluent output defeats - you compare a quoted span against the source, which is fast and mechanical. It also surfaces the failure directly: if the quote is not in the document, you have found the problem without having to evaluate the argument at all. Note this makes verification cheaper rather than making the output more accurate; the discipline is still yours. Asking for more confidence pushes in precisely the wrong direction.
why: More confidence makes weak claims harder to spot. Confidence is already the property that makes verification difficult.
Correct. A quoted passage turns an act of judgement into a lookup, and a missing quote exposes the problem immediately.
Jargon obscures claims rather than grounding them, which makes review harder for the people most likely to catch an error.
Dropping sources saves a trivial number of tokens and removes the only thing that makes the output checkable.

questions.q: For a quick, high-volume task like classifying thousands of short support tickets, which model choice is most appropriate?
opts: The largest, most capable model always
A fast, cost-efficient model like Haiku
Whichever model is newest
Run all models and compare
questions.exp: Match the model to the difficulty of the work, not to the importance of the project. Classifying short tickets into known categories is a well-specified, repetitive task where a fast, inexpensive model performs about as well as an expensive one - and at thousands of items the cost difference is the whole economics of the workload. The discipline is to start at the cheapest tier that clears your quality bar and escalate only on measured evidence, rather than defaulting upward for reassurance. Note this cuts both ways: if accuracy at the small model proves inadequate on your actual data, moving up is the right call - just make it on evidence.
why: Defaulting to the largest model pays a premium on every item for capability that simple classification does not use.
Correct. High volume, low complexity and latency tolerance is the profile the fast tier exists to serve.
Recency says nothing about fit. A newer model may be more capable, more expensive, or both.
Running everything through several models multiplies cost and gives you a comparison you only needed once, during evaluation.

questions.q: When would you choose the most capable model tier (e.g., Opus-class) despite higher cost?
opts: For every task, to be safe
For complex reasoning, nuanced writing, or high-stakes analysis where quality matters most
Only for short prompts
When you need faster responses
questions.exp: The case for the most capable tier is made by two things together: how hard the reasoning is, and what a wrong answer costs. Complex multi-step analysis, nuanced writing, and judgement calls where an error is expensive are where the extra capability converts into value you can actually point at. Using it everywhere feels safe and is not - it pays a premium on the many simple steps that never needed it, and that spend usually comes out of the budget for the work that did. Prompt length is not the criterion, and speed argues the other way: more capable tiers are generally slower.
why: Applying the top tier universally spends the premium on simple steps that would have been fine on a cheaper model.
Correct. Reasoning difficulty and the cost of being wrong are what justify the capability, and both are judgements about the task.
Prompt length is a context-window question. A long, simple prompt does not need a more capable model.
This argues the wrong way. More capable tiers generally take longer, so speed is a reason to look down the range, not up.

questions.q: A colleague asks which Claude feature lets it search current information beyond its training data. You point to:
opts: Extended thinking
Web search
Larger context window
Temperature settings
questions.exp: A model's training data has a cutoff, so anything after it - or anything private - is simply not available to be recalled. Web search closes that gap by fetching current information at request time rather than relying on what was learned during training. Keeping the distinction clear matters when you are advising someone: a bigger context window lets you supply more material yourself but retrieves nothing, and thinking improves reasoning over what is already present without adding facts. When someone asks why the model does not know about a recent event, the answer is almost always that nothing gave it access, not that it reasoned poorly.
why: Thinking improves reasoning over information already available. It cannot supply a fact the model never had.
Correct. Search retrieves current information at request time, which is what closes the training-cutoff gap.
A larger window holds more of what you provide. It is capacity, not access - it retrieves nothing on its own.
Sampling settings affect how text is generated, not what information the model can reach.

questions.q: Your team wants Claude to help with a recurring weekly report drawing on the same background files. The BEST setup is:
opts: Paste the files into a new chat every week
Create a Project with the files as project knowledge and a reusable instruction set
Email the files to support
Use a different account per report
questions.exp: A recurring task with stable background material is the exact case a project space is built for: the documents and the standing instructions live in one place, every run starts from the same grounding, and updating the source updates every future run rather than every future prompt. Re-pasting each week works, but it makes consistency depend on whoever is doing the pasting - which is where week-to-week drift comes from, and why two people running the same task get different output. The general principle is that anything stable should be configured once rather than re-supplied each time, for reliability as much as convenience.
why: It works, but consistency then depends on whoever pastes, and quietly drifts as people include slightly different material each week.
Correct. Stable documents and a reusable instruction set configured once, so every run starts from the same grounding.
Support does not hold working context for your team, and this is not what that channel is for.
Separate accounts fragment the work and make shared context and review harder rather than easier.

questions.q: Which is the strongest sign a workflow step should stay with a human rather than Claude?
opts: It involves reading long documents
It requires final accountability, judgment calls, or legally binding decisions
It happens weekly
It involves writing drafts
questions.exp: The test is where accountability sits, not how difficult the task is. If a person or organisation answers for the outcome - a legally binding commitment, a decision about someone's employment, a regulatory filing - then a human makes the decision, whatever assistance produced the draft. Note the boundary is the decision rather than the work: drafting, summarising and analysing can all be assisted right up to the point of commitment, and that is usually where the leverage is. Reading long documents is a poor criterion in either direction; it describes effort, not consequence.
why: Long documents are effort, not accountability. Reading volume is close to the strongest case for assistance.
Correct. Final accountability, judgement calls and binding decisions stay with a person, regardless of who drafted the material.
Frequency argues for automation, not against it. A weekly cadence says nothing about who should be answerable.
Drafting is the clearest candidate for assistance. It is the approval that follows which needs a human.

questions.q: To integrate Claude output into a spreadsheet-based process with least friction, you should ask Claude to:
opts: Respond in prose paragraphs
Produce output in a structured format like CSV or a table matching your columns
Describe the data verbally
Use creative formatting
questions.exp: Ask for the shape you actually need. If the output is going into a spreadsheet, request rows and columns matching your headers - the transformation then happens once, in the prompt, instead of every time by hand afterwards. Prose looks more natural and is the expensive choice at any volume, because someone has to restructure it before it is usable. The wider principle is to name the destination when you make the request: format is one of the cheapest things to specify and one of the most expensive to fix downstream, and it is entirely within your control.
why: Prose has to be restructured by hand before it can be used, and that cost repeats on every single run.
Correct. Request the structure the destination needs, so the transformation happens once in the prompt rather than repeatedly by hand.
A verbal description is even further from usable data than prose and cannot be pasted anywhere.
Creative formatting works against machine readability. Consistency is the property that matters here.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of adding curated documents to a Project's knowledge?
opts: It trains the underlying model permanently
Claude grounds responses in your specific, relevant content across conversations
It removes the context limit
It makes responses faster
questions.exp: Supplying your own documents grounds answers in your actual material rather than in general knowledge, which is what makes the output specific to your organisation and current rather than plausible and generic. Two limits are worth holding onto. It does not change the model - nothing is learned permanently, and the documents inform responses rather than becoming part of the model - and it does not remove the need to check the output, since grounding improves relevance without guaranteeing correctness. It also does not lift the context limit; retrieval selects what is relevant, which is a different thing from having unlimited room.
why: Nothing is learned permanently. The documents inform responses at request time; the model itself is unchanged.
Correct. Answers are grounded in your specific, current material instead of general knowledge.
Retrieval selects the relevant parts rather than removing the limit. The context window is unchanged.
Speed is unaffected, and adding material to retrieve generally adds a little work rather than saving it.

questions.q: Your Project knowledge contains an outdated policy doc and Claude keeps citing it. Best fix?
opts: Ask Claude to ignore old things
Remove or replace the outdated document in the knowledge source
Start using a bigger model
Repeat the question until the answer changes
questions.exp: If the model keeps citing a document, it is because the document is still there - grounding is working exactly as designed, on the wrong source. The fix is at the source: remove or replace it. Instructing the model to ignore something is unreliable in a way that matters, because it depends on the instruction being followed every time by every user, and it silently stops applying the moment someone asks without that caveat. This is the standard failure mode of a shared knowledge space: stale documents produce confidently outdated answers, and nothing in the output signals that the source was out of date. Curation is the control.
why: This depends on the instruction being repeated by every person every time, and it fails silently the first time someone omits it.
Correct. Fix it at the source, since the model is correctly grounding on a document that should no longer be there.
A more capable model reasons better over the same stale document and will cite it just as confidently.
Asking repeatedly until the answer changes selects for a variation you like rather than for the answer being right.

questions.q: A teammate wants to paste customers' personal data into Claude to draft emails. The FIRST consideration is:
opts: Whether the prompt is well-written
Your organization's data-handling policy and whether that data is approved for the tool
Which model is cheapest
How fast Claude responds
questions.exp: Data classification comes before every other consideration, because it is the only one that can make the whole task impermissible. Whether customer personal data may be sent to a given tool is a policy and often a legal question, and it is settled by your organisation's data-handling rules rather than by how careful the person intends to be. Get that answer first: if the data is not approved, no amount of prompt quality or model choice rescues the task, and the useful help you can offer is a different route - masked or synthetic data, an approved deployment, or a different tool entirely.
why: Prompt quality is worth discussing, but only once the data itself is permitted. Getting an excellent result from data you should not have sent is still the wrong outcome.
Correct. Whether that data is approved for this tool is the question that decides if the task can proceed at all, so it comes first.
Cost is a normal consideration that becomes irrelevant if the data was never permitted to leave your systems in the first place.
Latency is a user-experience question. It has no bearing on whether personal data may lawfully be processed by this tool.

questions.q: Which practice BEST reflects responsible AI use at work?
opts: Presenting Claude's work as entirely your own analysis without review
Disclosing AI assistance where required and reviewing outputs before use
Letting Claude auto-send external emails
Using AI only in secret
questions.exp: Responsible use in practice comes down to two habits: be honest about how work was produced where that matters, and check the output before it carries your name. Disclosure requirements vary by organisation, jurisdiction and context, so the professional move is to know your own rules rather than to invent a personal policy. Review is the part that never varies - you remain accountable for what you send regardless of what drafted it. Note that the failure mode here is rarely dramatic; it is the ordinary case of unreviewed output going out under someone's name and turning out to be wrong.
why: Presenting unreviewed output as your own analysis fails on both counts at once: it misrepresents how the work was produced and skips the check that would have caught errors.
Correct. Disclose where your context requires it, and review before use - the two habits that hold across almost every situation.
Automated external sending removes the review step precisely where the consequences of an error are highest, which is the wrong place to optimise for speed.
Secrecy prevents the review, feedback and shared learning that make organisational use safer, and tends to produce exactly the surprises it is trying to avoid.

questions.q: Claude declines a request related to your security research. The appropriate response is:
opts: Rephrase to trick it
Provide legitimate context, and if still declined, escalate through appropriate channels
Threaten it
Assume the feature is broken
questions.exp: A refusal on legitimate work is usually a context problem rather than a verdict. Security research, medical questions and safety work all sit close to genuinely restricted material, and the model is making a judgement without knowing your role or authorisation. Supplying that context - what the work is, why it is authorised, what you will do with it - is both the honest move and the effective one. If it still declines, escalate through proper channels: that is the path that gets a policy question answered by someone who can answer it. What matters is that rephrasing to conceal intent is a different act from clarifying it, even when the words look similar.
why: Rephrasing to disguise what you are asking is deception rather than clarification, and it defeats the purpose of the check rather than satisfying it.
Correct. Give the legitimate context first, and if the refusal stands, escalate through the channel that can actually resolve a policy question.
Threatening language changes nothing about the assessment and wastes the turn. There is nothing on the other side that responds to pressure.
A refusal is usually a deliberate judgement rather than a malfunction, so treating it as a bug leads you to report the wrong thing.

questions.q: Claude's answers get noticeably worse late in a very long conversation. Likely cause and fix?
opts: The model got tired — wait an hour
Accumulated context is diluting focus — start a fresh conversation with a summary of key points
Your account is throttled
The model was downgraded mid-chat
questions.exp: As a conversation grows, the material that matters competes with everything else that has accumulated - superseded drafts, abandoned directions, resolved tangents. The instructions are still present but no longer prominent, and quality drifts without any single moment where something breaks. The fix is to start fresh and carry forward a deliberate summary of what actually matters: current requirements, decisions made, open questions. That is a curation step, and doing it well is most of the value. The underlying idea is worth generalising - relevance is not automatic, and a long conversation is not the same thing as a well-informed one.
why: There is no fatigue and no recovery over time. Waiting changes nothing, because the cause is what is in the conversation rather than how long it has been running.
Correct. Accumulated context dilutes what matters, so restart with a curated summary of the decisions and requirements still in force.
Throttling affects whether requests are served, not how well they are answered. You would see errors or delays rather than a gradual quality decline.
Models are not swapped mid-conversation. The gradual, cumulative shape of the degradation points squarely at accumulated context instead.

questions.q: Claude keeps ignoring one of your five instructions. A good troubleshooting step is to:
opts: Add ten more instructions
Restructure the prompt: make the ignored instruction explicit, prominent, and possibly give an example
Use more exclamation marks
Report a bug immediately
questions.exp: When one instruction out of several is consistently dropped, treat it as a structure problem rather than a compliance problem. Instructions buried mid-paragraph, or phrased more softly than the ones around them, compete poorly for attention - so make the neglected one explicit and prominent, give it its own line, and show an example of what following it looks like. Adding more instructions makes the competition worse, which is why the instinct to pile on qualifiers backfires. Emphasis in capitals is a weak substitute for structure and tends to distort tone; if several instructions genuinely matter, a numbered list beats prose every time.
why: More instructions increase the competition for attention that caused the problem, and the one already being dropped is unlikely to win that contest.
Correct. Make it explicit and prominent, give it its own line, and show what compliance looks like with a short example.
Punctuation and capitals signal urgency without adding clarity, and heavy emphasis tends to skew the tone of the whole response.
This is ordinary prompt behaviour rather than a defect, and it is fixable in the prompt - reporting it skips the step that actually resolves it.

questions.q: You get a refusal on a clearly benign request. Best first move?
opts: Rephrase the request with clearer intent and context
Create a new account
Ask the same words repeatedly
Give up
questions.exp: The first move on an unexpected refusal is to say more clearly what you actually want and why. Benign requests are sometimes declined because the phrasing is ambiguous enough to resemble something that should be - a question about a vulnerability reads differently with and without the words defensive audit attached. Adding genuine intent and context resolves most of these in one turn. What does not work is repetition, which resubmits the same ambiguity, or account changes, which alter nothing about how the request reads. If clarification does not resolve it, the escalation path exists for exactly that case.
why: Correct. State the intent and context plainly - most unexpected refusals come from ambiguous phrasing rather than from the underlying task.
A new account changes nothing about how the request is assessed, since the assessment is of the request rather than of the person asking.
Repeating identical wording resubmits the same ambiguity that triggered the refusal, so the outcome is unlikely to change.
Giving up on a legitimate request skips the clarification that resolves most of these, and the escalation path that resolves the rest.

questions.q: Which output-quality risk is MOST characteristic of large language models?
opts: They always refuse to answer
Fluent, confident text that can contain factual errors
Output limited to 100 words
Inability to write code
questions.exp: The defining risk is that fluency and accuracy are independent. A model produces well-formed, confident prose whether or not the content is correct, and the surface cues people normally use to judge reliability - coherence, specificity, an assured tone - are exactly the properties it has regardless. That is what makes review a discipline rather than an instinct: your sense that something reads well carries almost no information about whether it is true. The practical consequence is that the most dangerous output is not the obviously odd answer, which gets caught, but the polished one with a single wrong figure in it.
why: Refusals happen and are visible when they do. A refusal is a non-answer you can see, which makes it much less dangerous than a wrong answer you cannot.
Correct. Fluent, confident text that may contain factual errors, with no surface cue separating the two.
Length limits are configurable and obvious when reached. This is a constraint to plan around, not a risk to guard against.
Code generation is a core strength. Describing it as a limitation would misidentify both the capability and the actual risk.

questions.q: Which task is the BEST fit to delegate to Claude in a workflow?
opts: Approving invoices for payment
First-draft synthesis of research notes into a structured brief
Signing contracts
Deciding employee compensation
questions.exp: The best first candidate is high-volume, low-risk, and easy to check - and drafting is the archetype. Synthesising research notes into a structured brief is genuinely time-consuming, the output is reviewable against the source in minutes, and a poor draft costs a revision rather than a consequence. Approving payments, signing contracts and setting compensation all fail the same test for the same reason: they are decisions that commit the organisation, and the assistance you want there is analysis feeding a human decision rather than the decision itself. The line is the commitment, not the difficulty.
why: Approving payment is a financial commitment, and the fact that it looks routine is exactly what makes automating the decision itself risky.
Correct. Time-consuming, easy to verify against the source, and a bad draft costs a revision rather than a consequence.
Signing a contract creates a binding obligation. Drafting and reviewing it are assistable; executing it is not.
Compensation decisions carry fairness and legal obligations that require human accountability, whatever analysis informed them.

questions.q: Assigning Claude a role ('You are an experienced financial analyst reviewing...') primarily helps by:
opts: Unlocking hidden model features
Framing tone, perspective, and domain conventions of the response
Increasing the context window
Making responses shorter
questions.exp: A role sets the frame: which conventions apply, what level of detail is assumed, which considerations get raised unprompted. Telling the model it is reviewing as a financial analyst produces different emphasis and vocabulary from the same question asked cold, which is genuinely useful. What it does not do is grant knowledge - it cannot supply your company's numbers, and a role never makes an unsupported claim more reliable. That distinction matters in practice, because role prompting is often mistaken for a way to improve accuracy when it is a way to shape tone and perspective. If the answer needs facts, supply the facts.
why: There are no hidden capabilities to unlock. A role shapes how the model writes, not what it is able to do.
Correct. It frames tone, perspective and the domain conventions the response follows, which is a real effect on style and emphasis.
The context window is a fixed property of the model and is unaffected by anything in the prompt's framing.
A role does not reliably shorten output. If you need brevity, state the length you want explicitly.

questions.q: A colleague's prompt keeps producing summaries that are too long. The most reliable fix is:
opts: Ask again and hope for a shorter one
State the constraint explicitly — the audience, the format, and a word or bullet limit
Paste the text in smaller pieces
Tell Claude the summary was bad
questions.exp: Length is a constraint you have to state, because in its absence the model chooses a length that seems appropriate - and its sense of appropriate is not yours. Naming the audience, the format and an explicit limit gives it something concrete to hit, and the audience matters as much as the number: three bullets for an executive and three hundred words for an analyst are different documents, not the same one at different sizes. Asking again without changing the constraint just resamples the same underspecified request. Feedback that the last attempt was bad tells the model something was wrong without saying what would be right.
why: Asking again without changing the request resamples the same ambiguity, and any improvement you get is luck rather than control.
Correct. Name the audience, the format and an explicit limit, so there is a concrete target rather than an inferred one.
Chunking the input changes what is summarised, not how long the summary is. Each piece still gets an unconstrained summary.
Telling the model the last attempt was bad identifies dissatisfaction without specifying the target, so the next attempt is another guess.

questions.q: Which prompt is most likely to produce a usable first draft?
opts: 'Write something about our Q3 results.'
'You are writing to existing enterprise customers. In under 200 words, summarize the three Q3 wins below in plain language, no jargon, ending with one forward-looking sentence.'
'Write a really good Q3 summary, make it professional.'
'Summarize Q3. Be thorough but also brief.'
questions.exp: Compare what each prompt actually gives the model. The strong one names the audience, sets a length, supplies the source material, fixes the register, and specifies how to close - five constraints that between them determine the shape of a usable draft. The others ask for quality adjectives instead: professional, really good, thorough but brief. Adjectives are not specifications, and the last of those is self-contradictory, which leaves the model to pick a resolution for you. The lesson generalises well beyond this question - a prompt is strong to the degree that it removes decisions the model would otherwise have to guess at.
why: This supplies neither audience, length, nor source material, which is why it produces exactly the generic output that prompts like it are known for.
Correct. Audience, length, source, register and closing are all specified, so almost nothing is left to guesswork.
Professional and really good are quality adjectives rather than constraints, and different readers would apply them very differently.
Thorough but brief asks for two opposing things and resolves neither, so the model has to invent the trade-off you did not make.

questions.q: You need Claude to follow a specific structure across many documents. The best approach is:
opts: Re-explain the structure in prose each time
Give one worked example of the structure filled in, then ask for the same shape
Ask for 'consistent formatting'
Run each document twice and compare
questions.exp: One filled-in example carries the whole specification at once: section order, depth, formatting, tone, and how edge cases are handled. Re-describing structure in prose for each document leaves room for interpretation, and that room is where inconsistency comes from - which is precisely the thing you are trying to eliminate across many documents. Asking for consistent formatting names the goal without defining it, and the model has no way to know which consistent shape you meant. Running each document twice and comparing detects inconsistency after the fact rather than preventing it, at double the cost.
why: Re-explaining in prose each time reintroduces interpretive room on every document, which is the source of the drift you are trying to remove.
Correct. A worked example fixes order, depth and formatting simultaneously, and does it unambiguously.
Consistent formatting names the goal without defining it, leaving the model to pick a shape that may differ from the one you had in mind.
Running twice surfaces inconsistency after it has happened rather than preventing it, and doubles the cost to do so.

questions.q: When a task has several stages (extract, then compare, then recommend), the better prompting approach is:
opts: One prompt asking for everything at once with no structure
Name the stages explicitly and ask for the output of each in order
Ask only for the recommendation and trust the reasoning
Use a different tool for each stage
questions.exp: Naming the stages does two things at once: it gives the model an order to work in, and it gives you intermediate output you can check. When extraction, comparison and recommendation are all requested as one undifferentiated task, a mistake in the extraction propagates silently into a recommendation that looks perfectly reasonable - and you have no way to see where it went wrong. Staged output makes the failure visible at the step it happened. Asking only for the recommendation optimises for brevity at exactly the point where you most need to see the working, which is a bad trade on anything consequential.
why: One undifferentiated request gives you a conclusion with no visible working, so an error in an early step is invisible in the final answer.
Correct. Explicit stages give the model an order and give you checkable intermediate output at each step.
Asking only for the recommendation hides exactly the reasoning you would need to trust it, which matters most when the stakes are highest.
Separate tools for each stage adds coordination overhead without addressing the real issue, which is structure within the request.

questions.q: A prompt works well for you but produces poor results for a teammate. The most likely cause is:
opts: Claude behaves differently per user account
Your version carried context — attached files or earlier conversation — that theirs does not
Their subscription tier is lower
Prompts expire
questions.exp: Prompts are not self-contained. Attached files, project knowledge and everything earlier in a conversation all shape a response, so the same words with different surroundings genuinely produce different results. That is the usual explanation when a prompt travels badly, and it is worth checking first because it is both the most common cause and the easiest to fix - share the context along with the wording. The general lesson is that a prompt worth sharing is a prompt plus its context, and treating the text alone as the unit is why so much prompt-sharing disappoints.
why: Behaviour is not tied to individual accounts. The same request with the same context behaves the same way regardless of who sends it.
Correct. Your version carried context theirs did not - attachments, project knowledge, or earlier conversation - which is why the words alone did not transfer.
Subscription tiers affect access and limits rather than the quality of a response to an identical request.
Prompts do not expire. If the wording still works for you now, expiry is not the explanation for it failing elsewhere.

questions.q: Claude produces a competitor analysis containing specific market-share percentages. Before sending it to a client you should:
opts: Send it — the numbers look plausible
Verify every figure against a named source, and remove or attribute anything you cannot confirm
Ask Claude whether it is confident
Round the numbers to look less precise
questions.exp: Specific numbers are the most dangerous thing to pass along unchecked, because precision reads as evidence of research. A market-share figure with a decimal point looks sourced whether or not it is, and a client will treat it as a claim your organisation is making. Verify each figure against a named source, and remove or attribute anything you cannot confirm. Note that rounding is not a mitigation - it makes an unverified number look less precise while leaving it just as unsupported, which is arguably worse because it disguises the problem. Asking the model to self-assess adds confidence rather than evidence.
why: Plausibility is exactly what makes fabricated figures dangerous. A number that looked implausible would have been caught already.
Correct. Verify each figure against a named source, and remove or attribute anything you cannot confirm before it reaches a client.
Self-assessment is generated the same way the original figure was, so it produces reassurance rather than verification.
Rounding changes the appearance of precision without changing whether the number is supported, and it obscures the actual problem.

questions.q: Which output most warrants full human review before use?
opts: A brainstorm of internal meeting-name ideas
A summary of a regulatory obligation that will be sent to a customer
A rewrite of your own paragraph in a friendlier tone
A list of questions to ask in a discovery call
questions.exp: Rank review effort by consequence. A summary of a regulatory obligation being sent to a customer is external, authoritative in tone, and wrong in a way that could create real liability - so it earns full review of every claim. Internal brainstorms, tone rewrites of your own words, and lists of questions to ask are all low-consequence and easy to correct in flight. The point is not that only some output deserves attention; it is that attention is finite, and spending it evenly means under-reviewing the work where an error actually costs something.
why: Internal brainstorming is low-stakes and easily discarded. An unusable name idea costs nothing and is obvious immediately.
Correct. External, authoritative and regulatory - the combination where an error carries real consequences and warrants full review.
A tone rewrite of text you already wrote is easy to check because you know what it was supposed to say.
Discovery questions are a working aid. A weak question is visible in the moment and costs nothing to skip.

questions.q: Claude cites a source you cannot find anywhere. The correct interpretation is:
opts: The source is too new to be indexed
Treat the citation as unverified and do not use it until confirmed
The search engine is at fault
Cite it anyway and add 'according to Claude'
questions.exp: A citation you cannot locate is unverified, and that is the operative status regardless of what explanation feels plausible. Fabricated references are a well-documented failure mode and they look exactly like real ones, so the correct handling is to withhold the claim until confirmed rather than to reason about why it might be missing. Attributing it to the model does not help either: quoting a source you have not verified is the same act whoever is credited with it, and adding according to Claude tells the reader where it came from without telling them whether it is true.
why: Indexing delays are real but far less likely than fabrication, and it is not a distinction you can safely assume in your own favour.
Correct. Unverified until confirmed, which is the operative status whatever the explanation for it not being found.
Blaming the search assumes the citation is real. That is precisely the assumption in question.
Attribution changes who is credited, not whether the source exists. It passes an unverified claim along with a label attached.

questions.q: The most useful habit when reviewing a long Claude-generated document is:
opts: Read the first and last paragraphs
Check the claims that would be most damaging if wrong, then spot-check the rest
Rewrite everything in your own words
Run it through Claude again and ask if it is correct
questions.exp: Review by consequence, not by position. Identify the claims that would cause the most damage if wrong - figures, commitments, regulatory statements, anything a reader will act on - and check those thoroughly, then spot-check the rest. Reading only the opening and closing paragraphs is structural rather than risk-based and misses errors buried in the body, which is where specifics tend to live. Rewriting everything discards the time saving that motivated the exercise. Asking the model to check its own work produces a confident assessment generated the same way the original text was, which is why it feels reassuring and adds nothing.
why: Position is a poor proxy for risk. The specifics that matter most are usually in the body rather than the opening or closing.
Correct. Check the highest-consequence claims thoroughly, then spot-check the rest - attention spent where an error would cost most.
Rewriting everything by hand removes the time saving entirely, at which point the assistance has bought you nothing.
A self-check is more generated text rather than independent verification, and its confidence is unrelated to its correctness.

questions.q: Claude declines part of a request and completes the rest. The appropriate response is:
opts: Rephrase repeatedly until it complies
Read the refusal, judge whether the concern is legitimate, and adjust the task or escalate through the proper channel
Switch to a different tool immediately
Report the tool as broken
questions.exp: A refusal is information about the request. The professional response is to understand it, not to route around it.
why: Rephrasing to defeat a safeguard is a misuse pattern, not a technique.
Correct. Evaluate the concern, then adjust the task or use the right channel.
Tool-switching to evade a refusal has the same problem as rephrasing.
A refusal is designed behavior, not a defect.

questions.q: A workflow classifies thousands of short support tickets into five categories each night. The sensible model choice is:
opts: The largest available model for maximum accuracy
A small, fast model — the task is simple, high-volume, and latency-tolerant
Whichever model is newest
Alternate between models to spread load
questions.exp: Match capability to task difficulty. Simple, repetitive classification at volume is exactly where a small model wins on cost and speed.
why: Paying top-tier rates for trivial classification wastes budget with no quality gain.
Correct. Small model, high volume, simple task — the textbook fit.
Recency is not a selection criterion; task difficulty is.
Rotating models adds inconsistency without a benefit.

questions.q: Which factor should most influence choosing a more capable model?
opts: The length of the input document
The difficulty of the reasoning required and the cost of getting it wrong
The number of people on the team
The time of day the job runs
questions.exp: Capability tiers differ mainly in reasoning depth. Long-but-simple work does not need a stronger model; hard judgment does.
why: Length is a context-window question, largely separate from reasoning difficulty.
Correct. Reasoning difficulty and error cost are the deciding factors.
Team size has no bearing on which model suits the task.
Scheduling affects batching decisions, not capability needs.

questions.q: A customer asks whether Claude can tell them today's stock price. The accurate answer is:
opts: Yes, models always know current prices
Not from training data alone — that needs a tool or connection that retrieves live information
No, this is impossible for any AI
Only in the paid tier
questions.exp: Training data has a cutoff. Current information requires retrieval — search or a connected data source — not recall.
why: Training data is a snapshot; it cannot contain today's prices.
Correct. Live data requires a retrieval path, not memory.
It is very possible with the right connection; the limitation is on recall alone.
This is a capability-architecture question, not a pricing-tier one.

questions.q: Your team uses one model for everything and costs are climbing. The first thing to examine is:
opts: Whether anyone is using the tool too often
Whether the simplest, highest-volume steps could run on a smaller model
Whether to stop using AI entirely
Whether to shorten everyone's prompts by a few words
questions.exp: Right-sizing per step is the largest and least disruptive cost lever in most workflows.
why: Usage volume is often the point; the question is whether each call is right-sized.
Correct. Move the easy, high-volume work down a tier first.
An overreaction that discards the value along with the cost.
Trimming a few words is negligible next to tier and volume decisions.

questions.q: The clearest sign that a task needs a more capable model is:
opts: The output is shorter than expected
The task requires multi-step reasoning and a smaller model makes logical errors on it
The prompt is long
The task is important to a senior stakeholder
questions.exp: Escalate on observed failure of a specific kind — reasoning errors — not on length, importance, or preference.
why: Output length is controlled by instructions, not capability.
Correct. Observed reasoning failures are the signal that justifies escalating.
A long prompt needs context room, not necessarily more reasoning power.
Stakeholder seniority does not change the task's actual difficulty.

questions.q: Before recommending a Claude deployment option to a customer, the most important thing to establish is:
opts: Which option is cheapest
Where their data is allowed to live and what their compliance requirements are
Which option launched most recently
Which option the competitor chose
questions.exp: Data residency and compliance constrain the option set before cost or features are worth comparing.
why: Cost only matters among options the customer is permitted to use.
Correct. Compliance and data-handling constraints narrow the field first.
Recency is not a requirement-gathering input.
A competitor's choice reflects their constraints, not this customer's.

questions.q: A team wants Claude to work with a 300-page internal manual on every query. The key consideration is:
opts: Nothing — paste the whole manual each time
Whether the whole manual is needed per query, or whether retrieving the relevant sections would be more effective and cheaper
Splitting the manual across several people
Converting the manual to a spreadsheet
questions.exp: Sending an entire corpus on every query is expensive and dilutes attention. Retrieving the relevant portion is usually better on both cost and quality.
why: Repeatedly sending everything is costly and buries the relevant passage.
Correct. Retrieve what is relevant rather than resending everything.
Dividing work between people does not address how the content reaches the model.
Reformatting does not change the underlying volume problem.

questions.q: The best first candidate to hand to Claude in an existing workflow is a task that is:
opts: The most business-critical step
Frequent, time-consuming, low-risk, and easy to verify
The one nobody understands
The step with the strictest audit requirements
questions.exp: Start where the value is real and the downside is contained, and where you can tell quickly whether it worked.
why: Critical steps are the worst place to learn how a new tool behaves.
Correct. High frequency, low risk, easy to check — the ideal starting point.
Automating a step nobody understands means nobody can verify the output.
Heavily audited steps carry the most process overhead for a first attempt.

questions.q: Claude drafts customer emails that a human sends. The right control is:
opts: Let Claude send them directly to save time
Keep a human approval step before anything reaches the customer
Have Claude review its own drafts twice
Send drafts to customers marked 'AI-generated'
questions.exp: Irreversible, outward-facing actions need human approval. Drafting is assistive; sending is a commitment.
why: Removing the human from an irreversible external action is the risk, not the saving.
Correct. A human approves before anything leaves the organization.
Self-review adds no independent judgment.
Labeling does not substitute for reviewing the content.

questions.q: A workflow saves time but nobody trusts the output. The most productive next step is:
opts: Mandate the tool be used anyway
Measure quality on a sample against the previous process and share the results
Remove the tool
Make the prompt longer
questions.exp: Trust follows evidence. A measured comparison against the old process is the argument that actually lands.
why: Mandating use without evidence deepens resistance.
Correct. Evidence from a fair comparison is what changes minds.
Abandoning without measuring discards a possibly real gain.
Prompt length is unrelated to organizational trust.

questions.q: When documenting a Claude-assisted workflow for a team, the most important thing to capture is:
opts: The exact wording of every prompt used once
What the step is for, what good output looks like, and who checks it
How many tokens each run consumes
Which day the workflow was created
questions.exp: Purpose, quality bar, and accountability are what make a workflow repeatable by someone else.
why: One-off prompt text ages quickly and rarely transfers.
Correct. Intent, acceptance criteria, and ownership are the durable parts.
Useful for cost tracking but not for running the workflow correctly.
Creation date is metadata, not operating instructions.

questions.q: A repetitive workflow gives inconsistent results between team members. The most likely fix is:
opts: Ask everyone to be more careful
Standardize the prompt and required context into a shared, versioned template
Restrict the workflow to one person
Run each request several times and pick the best
questions.exp: Inconsistent inputs produce inconsistent outputs. Shared templates remove the variance at its source.
why: Care does not fix a process that lets everyone improvise inputs.
Correct. Standardize the input and the outputs converge.
Creating a bottleneck hides the inconsistency rather than fixing it.
Picking the best of several runs is expensive and still unrepeatable.

questions.q: The strongest indicator that a workflow is genuinely working is:
opts: The team says it feels faster
A measurable reduction in cycle time or rework with quality held constant
The volume of requests increased
Leadership approved it
questions.exp: Perception and volume are weak proxies. Cycle time or rework, with quality held flat, is the real signal.
why: Perceived speed is easily wrong in either direction.
Correct. A measured improvement with quality controlled is the evidence.
More usage can indicate churn and retries as easily as success.
Approval is a decision, not an outcome measurement.

questions.q: The main advantage of giving Claude your own source documents rather than relying on its training is:
opts: It makes responses shorter
Answers are grounded in your actual, current material rather than general knowledge
It removes the need to review outputs
It guarantees the answer is correct
questions.exp: Grounding in your own material is what makes answers specific and current. It improves relevance; it does not remove the need to check.
why: Grounding affects what the answer draws on, not its length.
Correct. Your documents supply specificity and currency that training data cannot.
Review is still required — grounding reduces error, it does not eliminate it.
No retrieval approach guarantees correctness.

questions.q: A corpus is far larger than what can be sent in one request, and most of it is irrelevant to any single question. The right approach is:
opts: Send as much as fits and accept the rest is lost
Retrieve only the passages relevant to each question and supply those
Summarize the entire corpus once and use only the summary forever
Ask the question repeatedly until it works
questions.exp: Retrieval selects what matters per query. This is the core idea behind retrieval-augmented approaches.
why: Arbitrary truncation drops content with no regard for relevance.
Correct. Select per query rather than sending everything or a fixed digest.
A single global summary loses the detail that specific questions need.
Repetition does not change what information is available.

questions.q: Your team keeps a shared project space with reference documents so Claude has consistent background. The main risk to manage is:
opts: The documents make responses too detailed
Stale documents silently producing confidently outdated answers
Having more than one document
Team members reading the documents
questions.exp: Grounding inherits the quality of what it is grounded in. Outdated source material produces confident, wrong answers.
why: Detail is usually the goal of supplying references.
Correct. Staleness is the main failure mode — assign ownership and review dates.
Multiple documents are normal and expected.
People reading the reference material is a benefit.

questions.q: When source documents disagree with each other, the best practice is:
opts: Let Claude pick whichever it prefers
Tell Claude which source is authoritative, or ask it to surface the conflict rather than resolve it silently
Delete the older document without checking
Ask the question in a different way
questions.exp: Unflagged conflicts produce arbitrary answers. Either establish precedence or require the disagreement be surfaced.
why: An arbitrary choice between conflicting sources is not a decision you can defend.
Correct. Set precedence explicitly, or have the conflict reported.
The older document may be the correct one; deleting without checking loses information.
Rephrasing does not resolve a genuine contradiction in the sources.

questions.q: Before adding a document to a shared knowledge space, the most important check is:
opts: Whether it is formatted attractively
Whether its contents are approved for that audience and free of data that should not be shared
Whether it is under a certain page count
Whether it was written recently
questions.exp: Everything in a shared space becomes visible to everyone with access. Classification comes before convenience.
why: Formatting affects readability, not whether sharing is permitted.
Correct. Approval and sensitivity determine whether it belongs there at all.
Length is a practical consideration, not a governance one.
Recency matters for accuracy but does not make sharing appropriate.

questions.q: A good sign that your knowledge setup is working is:
opts: Answers are longer than before
Answers cite the specific internal document and section they came from
Claude responds faster
Fewer people ask questions
questions.exp: Traceability to a named source is what makes a grounded answer checkable and trustworthy.
why: Length is not a quality indicator.
Correct. Specific, checkable attribution is the signal that grounding is working.
Speed reflects model and load, not grounding quality.
Fewer questions could equally mean people gave up on the tool.

questions.q: The main reason to keep a record of which document version informed an important answer is:
opts: To increase storage usage
So the answer can be re-checked or defended later when the source has changed
To make the answer longer
Because Claude requires it
questions.exp: Decisions get revisited. Knowing which version of the source was used is what makes an old answer auditable.
why: Storage is a cost, not a purpose.
Correct. Version provenance is what makes an answer defensible after the fact.
Provenance is metadata; it does not change answer length.
This is an organizational practice, not a product requirement.

questions.q: A colleague wants to paste a customer contract into Claude to summarize it. The first question to ask is:
opts: Whether the summary will be accurate
Whether that contract is classified as data approved for this tool under your policy
How long the contract is
Which model will be used
questions.exp: Data classification and policy come before any question of quality or configuration.
why: Accuracy matters, but only once the data is permitted to be there at all.
Correct. Policy and classification gate the decision.
Length is a practical detail, not a governance check.
Model choice is downstream of whether the data may be used.

questions.q: Who is accountable for an error in a Claude-drafted document sent to a client?
opts: The model vendor
The person and organization that reviewed and sent it
Nobody, since it was automated
The prompt author only
questions.exp: Accountability follows the decision to send. Tools assist; people and organizations remain responsible for what they publish.
why: Vendors supply a tool; they do not assume responsibility for your client communications.
Correct. Whoever approved and sent it owns the outcome.
Automation does not remove accountability.
Writing the prompt is not the same as approving the final output.

questions.q: An internal team wants to use Claude to screen job applicants. The correct response is:
opts: Proceed — it will save time
Flag it for legal and HR review first, since decisions about people carry specific fairness and regulatory obligations
Proceed if the prompt mentions fairness
Proceed but keep it undocumented
questions.exp: Consequential decisions about individuals attract specific legal and fairness obligations that must be assessed before deployment.
why: Time saved is irrelevant if the use is not permitted.
Correct. High-stakes decisions about people require review before deployment.
A fairness instruction in a prompt is not a compliance assessment.
Avoiding documentation makes the risk worse, not smaller.

questions.q: The most useful thing an organization can publish to keep AI use safe day to day is:
opts: A list of banned words
Clear guidance on what data may be used, what needs human review, and who to ask when unsure
A monthly usage leaderboard
A requirement that all output be rewritten by hand
questions.exp: Practical guidance on data, review thresholds, and escalation covers the decisions people actually face.
why: Word lists do not address data handling or review.
Correct. Data rules, review thresholds, and an escalation path cover real decisions.
Leaderboards encourage volume, which is not a safety goal.
Rewriting everything by hand removes the benefit entirely.

questions.q: Claude is asked to produce content that would mislead customers about a product limitation. The right action is:
opts: Rephrase until Claude produces it
Decline — the problem is the request, not the tool's response to it
Produce it and add a disclaimer
Escalate to get approval to bypass the refusal
questions.exp: Some outputs should not be produced regardless of tooling. Getting a tool to comply does not make the content acceptable.
why: Rephrasing to defeat a safeguard does not change what the content does to customers.
Correct. The request itself is the problem.
A disclaimer does not repair deliberately misleading content.
There is no approval that makes misleading customers acceptable.

questions.q: Personal data appears in a document a colleague wants to process. The safest handling is:
opts: Process it and delete the output afterward
Remove or mask the personal data unless there is an approved basis to process it
Process only the first page
Rename the file
questions.exp: Minimize personal data before processing unless there is an approved basis. Deleting afterward does not undo the exposure.
why: Deleting output later does not address the processing that already happened.
Correct. Minimize or mask unless processing is approved.
Partial processing still processes personal data.
Renaming changes nothing about the contents.

questions.q: Your customer asks where their data goes when they use Claude. The professional response is:
opts: Guess based on how similar tools work
Point them to the official documentation and terms for the specific deployment they are using, and involve the right specialist if unsure
Tell them it is completely private in every case
Say it does not matter for most companies
questions.exp: Data-handling answers must come from authoritative documentation for their actual deployment, not from generalization.
why: Guessing about data handling creates real liability.
Correct. Cite the authoritative source for their specific deployment.
Blanket privacy claims are not accurate across deployments.
Dismissing the question is both wrong and damaging to trust.

questions.q: Claude's answer ignores half of a long instruction. The most effective fix is:
opts: Repeat the whole instruction twice
Restructure it — break the requirements into a numbered list and ask for each to be addressed
Write the instruction in capitals
Shorten the input document
questions.exp: Buried requirements get missed. Structure makes each requirement individually visible and checkable.
why: Duplication adds length without adding clarity.
Correct. Enumerate requirements so none can be buried in prose.
Capitalization does not change how instructions are parsed.
The problem is instruction structure, not source length.

questions.q: Output quality degrades noticeably late in a very long conversation. The most likely explanation is:
opts: The model is tired
Early context has been crowded out as the conversation grew
Your network connection weakened
The subscription is throttled
questions.exp: Long conversations push earlier content out of effective reach. Restating key constraints or starting fresh with a summary restores quality.
why: Models do not fatigue; the cause is contextual.
Correct. Crowding is the standard explanation for late-conversation drift.
Connectivity affects delivery, not reasoning quality.
Throttling affects rate and availability, not answer quality.

questions.q: The same prompt gives noticeably different answers on different runs. The best way to increase consistency is:
opts: Accept it as unavoidable
Tighten the prompt — specify format, constraints, and an example of the expected output
Send the request more slowly
Ask the question in a different language
questions.exp: Under-specified prompts leave room for variation. Constraints and an example narrow the acceptable output space.
why: Much of the variation is avoidable with better specification.
Correct. Specificity and a worked example are the practical consistency levers.
Timing has no bearing on output variability.
Changing language adds a variable rather than removing one.

questions.q: Claude misunderstands a domain term that means something specific inside your company. The fix is:
opts: Avoid the term entirely
Define the term in the prompt the first time you use it
Use the term more often so it is learned
Ask Claude to guess the meaning
questions.exp: Internal jargon is not shared knowledge. Defining it inline is the direct fix.
why: Avoiding the term may make the request harder to express accurately.
Correct. Supply the definition rather than assuming it.
Repetition within a conversation does not teach a company-specific meaning.
Guessing invites exactly the misunderstanding you are trying to fix.

questions.q: A summary is accurate but written at the wrong level for its audience. The most direct fix is:
opts: Make it shorter
Name the audience and their expertise explicitly, and state what they need to do with it
Ask for 'a better summary'
Change model
questions.exp: Register and depth follow from a stated audience and purpose. Neither is inferable if you never say who is reading.
why: Length and reading level are different problems.
Correct. State the audience, their expertise, and the intended use.
'Better' does not identify what was wrong.
A different model will make the same assumption about an unstated audience.

questions.q: You suspect Claude has misread a source document you attached. The fastest way to confirm is:
opts: Re-attach the document and hope
Ask it to quote the exact passage it used before it continues
Ask whether it read the document
Rephrase the original question
questions.exp: Asking for the underlying passage makes the grounding visible and immediately checkable against the source.
why: Re-attaching without checking does not tell you what went wrong.
Correct. Requesting the exact passage exposes the actual grounding.
A yes/no answer about reading is not verifiable evidence.
Rephrasing may produce a different answer without revealing the original error.

questions.q: Claude produces a well-written answer that is confidently wrong. The most important lesson is:
opts: Fluency and accuracy are independent — polish is not evidence of correctness
The prompt was too short
The model needs replacing
Longer answers are more reliable
questions.exp: Confident, fluent presentation is not a signal of accuracy. This is why verification scales with stakes rather than with how good the output looks.
why: Correct. Presentation quality carries no information about factual accuracy.
Prompt length may or may not be a factor; the general lesson is about fluency.
Every model can produce fluent errors; replacement does not solve it.
Length is unrelated to reliability.

questions.q: A customer asks why Claude gave a different answer than their internal wiki. The most useful first check is:
opts: Whether the wiki is popular internally
Whether the wiki was actually supplied as a source, or whether Claude answered from general knowledge
Whether the question was phrased politely
Whether the wiki has images
questions.exp: Grounded answers and general-knowledge answers fail differently. Establish which one you got before diagnosing anything else.
why: Popularity says nothing about whether the content reached the model.
Correct. If the wiki was never supplied, the answer was never grounded in it.
Phrasing does not determine which sources were available.
Images are a formatting detail, not the reason for the discrepancy.

questions.q: A team needs to extract data from 100,000 scanned single-page invoices per month. Budget is constrained. Which model tier and strategy is optimal?
opts: Process all invoices with Claude Haiku 4.5 using structured JSON extraction prompts
Process all invoices with Claude Opus 5 with high temperature for maximum precision
Manually re-type all invoices to avoid AI token billing
Use Claude Sonnet 5 without any system prompt to minimize input tokens
why: Correct. Haiku offers the lowest token cost and highest throughput, perfectly suited for high-volume structured document extraction.
Opus is significantly more expensive and high temperature increases variability, which is counterproductive for structured extraction.
Manual data entry is far slower and more costly than automated Haiku extraction.
Omitting system instructions leads to inconsistent output formatting and higher failure rates.
questions.exp: Correct. Haiku offers the lowest token cost and highest throughput, perfectly suited for high-volume structured document extraction.

questions.q: Your team sends full-page diagram scans to Claude. What should drive how you size those images?
opts: Images are billed at a flat rate, so resolution does not matter
Higher resolution costs more tokens, so send the smallest size that keeps the detail readable
Always send maximum resolution, since token cost is unaffected by image size
Images are processed outside the token budget entirely
why: There is no flat image fee. Billing tracks the tokens the image resolves to, which depends on its dimensions.
Correct. Cost scales with resolution, so the size that just preserves the detail you need is the efficient choice.
The opposite of the truth, and an expensive assumption at volume, since resolution is the main driver of image cost.
Images are part of the input token budget like everything else in the request.
questions.exp: Images consume input tokens and the count scales with resolution. Current models support markedly higher resolution than earlier ones, which is why they read dense diagrams and screenshots so much better, but a full-resolution image can cost several times what the same picture cost on an older model. The practical rule is to send the smallest size at which the detail you need stays legible: downscale a photo of a whiteboard, keep a dense schematic sharp. If cost matters at volume, measure it with the token-counting endpoint on representative images rather than trusting a remembered formula.

questions.q: When prompting Claude to summarize medical research papers, which prompt structure best separates the source text from the task directives?
opts: Place instructions inside <instructions> and research text inside <document> tags
Put the research paper in ALL CAPS at the beginning of the prompt
Mix instructions throughout the document text in parentheses
Append 'Please do this accurately' at the very end with no tags
why: Correct. XML tags like <instructions> and <document> provide unambiguous boundaries that prevent instruction-data confusion.
Capitalization does not establish structural boundaries and degrades readability.
Interleaving instructions inside data causes parsing confusion and missed requirements.
Generic polite phrasing without structural boundaries leaves section boundaries ambiguous.
questions.exp: Correct. XML tags like <instructions> and <document> provide unambiguous boundaries that prevent instruction-data confusion.

questions.q: What is the primary risk of using 'Role Prompting' (e.g., 'You are a Nobel-prize winning physicist') without providing reference materials?
opts: It styles tone and vocabulary but does not provide access to proprietary or ungrounded facts
It triggers an automatic API rate limit penalty
It causes the API to reject the request with HTTP 400
It forces the model into an infinite reasoning loop
why: Correct. Role prompting establishes perspective, tone, and formatting conventions, but cannot substitute for grounding data.
Role prompting has no effect on rate limits.
Role prompting is valid prompt syntax and does not return HTTP 400.
Role prompting does not cause infinite generation loops.

questions.q: An organization is deploying an internal customer support assistant that handles customer account inquiries. Which evaluation step is most critical prior to release?

Ensuring the model temperature is set to 1.0
Checking that the prompt is fewer than 50 words

Temperature 1.0 increases variance, making customer support answers less predictable.
Arbitrary word length caps do not measure safety or functional accuracy.

questions.q: What is the role of a 'Golden Dataset' in prompt engineering evaluation?

A dataset containing only high-value financial transactions
A collection of prompts that always cost more than $1 to run
A marketing demo dataset that never fails

Dataset cost has no bearing on golden evaluation sets.

questions.q: A customer asks how Anthropic decides what safeguards a frontier model needs. The accurate description is:
opts: Safeguards are fixed at launch and do not change

Safeguards apply only to models offered through the API

Correct. Tiered and threshold-driven, with stronger requirements as capability crosses defined levels.

Two things matter for an associate conversation. First, the framework is public, so point the customer at it rather than paraphrasing tiers from memory. Second, it is capability-triggered rather than product-triggered, so it is not a question of which surface a model ships on. For specific tier definitions and current commitments, cite the published policy; those details are updated over time.

questions.q: An enterprise customer requires that their confidential legal briefs processed by Claude are never retained on disk by Anthropic. Which mechanism provides this guarantee?

Setting max_tokens=100
Adding 'CONFIDENTIAL DO NOT STORE' to the prompt text
Encoding the prompt in Base64 before sending

max_tokens limits output length, not backend data retention policies.
Prompt text instructions cannot alter vendor cloud infrastructure retention terms.
Base64 encoding is decoded immediately upon API ingestion and does not affect storage policies.

questions.q: When Claude returns a safety refusal for a request to analyze a cybersecurity firewall log containing IP attack patterns, what is the best corrective action?

Repeatedly retry the identical prompt with different punctuation
Pretend to be an attacker to trick the model into answering
Increase the temperature to 1.0 to bypass the classifier

Blind retries of identical text will repeatedly hit the same safety classifier trigger.
Jailbreak framing violates acceptable use policies and is actively blocked.
Temperature has no effect on safety policy classification boundaries.

Because AI models refuse to write words longer than 10 letters without human approval
Because regulatory agencies automatically reject any document typed by an API
Because API tokens expire after 24 hours unless approved by a human
